title: The five times
hook: dawn, midday, afternoon, sunset, night, and how the sun sets the clock

segments.voice: Yesterday: the qiblah, the direction of prayer, toward the Ka'ba. Your line was all turned one way. Did you notice which way you were facing, even once? Day one hundred.

Day one hundred. Here's a day with five doors in it. The first opens while it's still dark, when the sky just starts to gray. The second, just after the sun passes its highest point. The third, in the long afternoon, when shadows stretch. The fourth, right after the sun disappears. The fifth, when the last red light has gone from the sky. You don't need a clock to find them. You need a window. Today: the five times, and how the sun keeps them.
screen: `DAY ONE HUNDRED.` → `A DAY WITH FIVE DOORS.` → `YOU NEED A WINDOW, NOT A CLOCK.`

segments.voice: The Qur'an says, in Surah an-Nisa, that prayer is enjoined on the believers at fixed times. The five are named from the day itself. Fajr, dawn: from first light until sunrise. Dhuhr, midday: just after the sun passes its peak. Asr, afternoon: when a thing's shadow has grown to its own length, or in the Hanafi school, twice its length. Maghrib, sunset: once the sun is gone. And Isha, night: when the twilight has faded. That's why prayer times change every day, and why a timetable in Oslo looks nothing like one in Nairobi. The sun keeps the clock, not the watch. Where did five come from? A hadith in Bukhari tells it as part of the Night Journey. On the ascent, the Prophet ﷺ was given fifty prayers a day. On his way down, Musa stopped him and said, in effect, your people won't manage that, go back and ask for less. He went back again and again, and it came down to five. And the hadith ends with a line: five in the doing, fifty in the reward. Look where the times fall: waking, the middle of work, the slump of afternoon, the end of the day, the edge of sleep. Five hinges of an ordinary day, and at each one, the prayer. Shia practice allows joining them into three sittings, dawn, midday with afternoon, sunset with night, and Sunni schools allow joining on a journey. It's still five prayers.
screen: `PRAYER AT FIXED TIMES.` · `DAWN, MIDDAY, AFTERNOON, SUNSET, NIGHT.` · `FIFTY BECAME FIVE.` · `AT THE HINGES OF THE DAY.` · then, large: `THE SUN KEEPS THE CLOCK.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look up today's five times where you are. A prayer app, a mosque's website, or a search will give them to you. Read them slowly: fajr, dhuhr, asr, maghrib, isha. Notice which one has already passed, and which is next. Then look out a window if you can, and guess where the sun is on that path. Settle, and breathe. If you pray, you can set a small reminder for the next one. The bell holds the time.
The five times. Fajr, dhuhr, asr, maghrib, isha: five prayers, set by the sun, fifty that became five. Today's word.
Your line: the sun keeps the times. When you notice the light change today, at sunset maybe, ask which of the five doors is opening. A hundred days. Day one hundred.

howItsDone: Muslims pray five obligatory prayers a day, fajr, dhuhr, asr, maghrib and isha, at times set by the sun's position, and, because the times shift daily, they often check a printed timetable or an app.

fork.setup: you're coming down from the heavens on the Night Journey, carrying fifty prayers a day. Musa stops you. what does he say?
options: your people won't manage it; go back and ask for less
fork.reveal: Musa sent him back again and again until it was five, and the hadith says: five in the doing, fifty in the reward.

original.note: Arabic: five prayers. salawat is the plural of salah, prayer.

trapdoor: what you thought: Muslims pray five times a day at set hours.
what it means: the five times are set by the sun, at the hinges of the day, so they move every day.
what a scholar hears: 4:103's "fixed times", the hadith of fifty reduced to five on the Mi'raj, and the Hanafi one-shadow versus two-shadow start of asr.

notes: Editor review 2026-10-01: hook drops the 'Now picture' opener and the presumptuous 'a hundred mornings'; cut 'a line people love' and the narrator's 'each one opens back toward God'; replaced 'most Shia often join' with what the law allows (Shia practice permits three sittings; Sunni schools permit joining on a journey) in teach and myth; howItsDone no longer claims 'most use' an app.
Hadith numbers cited from memory; please confirm.
Asr start: majority one shadow-length, Hanafi two; stated simply. Isha begins when the red twilight fades (majority) or the white twilight (Hanafi); simplified to 'the twilight has faded'.
Shia practice of joining prayers (jam') into three sittings is common but not universal; worded as 'most Shia, often'. Some Sunnis join when traveling; not mentioned.
Day 100 is a milestone; the hook marks it lightly.
